trust_boundaries: TB-1 Internet -> Ingress Layer: unauthenticated tenant traffic crosses from the public internet into API Gateway
TB-2 Ingress Layer -> LLM Service Layer: tenant-scoped request from Tenant Router enters the shared multi-tenant LLM Orchestrator
TB-3 LLM Service Layer -> Model Backends: confidential prompt and retrieved context leave platform control to OpenAI/Anthropic third-party APIs
TB-4 LLM Service Layer -> Data Layer: orchestrator compute gains read/write access to confidential conversation, vector and audit stores
TB-5 Tenant <-> Tenant isolation boundary inside the shared orchestrator, vector index namespace and conversation store
TB-6 Model Backend internal boundary: self-hosted LLM inference host sits on the platform network and consumes fine-tuned model artifacts
architecture_summary.operational_context: Multi-tenant SaaS deployed on public cloud (multi-region), agentic LLM pipeline with semi-autonomous per-request orchestration, hybrid model backend strategy (two third-party inference APIs plus one self-hosted fine-tuned model), shared data layer with logical tenant partitioning.

threat_actors.name: Opportunistic LLM Abuser
threat_actors.motivation: Financial gain through API cost abuse, free inference, and resale of harvested credentials; low-effort disruption.
threat_actors.initial_access_vector: Unauthenticated or self-registered access to the public API Gateway, automated abuse of LLM endpoints, and credential stuffing against tenant login.
non_capabilities: No physical access to cloud regions or data centers
No zero-day or exploit-development budget; relies on public tooling and known CVEs
No pre-existing tenant credentials or insider knowledge of tenant IDs
Cannot modify model weights, fine-tuning data, or self-hosted inference binaries
Cannot compromise upstream OpenAI or Anthropic infrastructure

threat_actors.name: Targeted Data Broker / Cybercriminal Group
threat_actors.motivation: Exfiltrate multi-tenant conversation and document data for resale, competitive intelligence, or extortion.
threat_actors.initial_access_vector: Phishing or infostealer compromise of tenant API keys and session tokens, followed by authenticated abuse of the Tenant Router and orchestrator.
non_capabilities: No nation-state SIGINT, upstream telco, or cloud-provider-level access
Cannot read per-tenant encryption keys held in the KMS
Cannot alter WORM/immutable audit storage directly
No physical access and no ability to persist inside managed third-party model providers
Cannot forge signed model artifacts accepted by the self-hosted inference host

threat_actors.name: Malicious or Over-Reaching Tenant Insider
threat_actors.motivation: Access competitor tenant data, exceed contractual data-retention scope, or extract proprietary prompt/RAG content.
threat_actors.initial_access_vector: Legitimate tenant account or tenant admin credentials used to probe cross-tenant retrieval, prompt injection, and orchestrator parameter manipulation.
non_capabilities: No host, network, or hypervisor layer access
No ability to read other tenants' encryption keys or KMS grants
No ability to write directly to the audit log store or disable platform logging
No control over model provider infrastructure or model weights
No ability to modify Prompt Guard or Response Filter source code

threat_actors.name: Model Supply-Chain Poisoner
threat_actors.motivation: Establish persistent, hard-to-detect influence over model outputs for a specific tenant or topic.
threat_actors.initial_access_vector: Compromise of the fine-tuning dataset or model artifact consumed by the Self-Hosted LLM, or poisoning of documents ingested into the Vector Database.
non_capabilities: No access to OpenAI or Anthropic model weights or training pipelines
Cannot merge code into Prompt Guard or Response Filter without passing code review
No physical access to the inference host
Cannot bypass signed-artifact verification once enforced
No ability to alter audit log retention or SIEM ingestion

attack_paths.entry_point: Public HTTPS API endpoint exposed to the internet (TB-1)
attack_paths.impact: Remote code execution or request smuggling in the gateway, leading to bypass of Rate Limiter and Tenant Router and direct access to the LLM Service Layer.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Gateway is internet-facing and continuously scanned, but a managed gateway with patched dependencies and WAF coverage reduces exploitability.

attack_paths.entry_point: Stolen tenant API key or session token replayed against the API Gateway (TB-1, TB-2)
attack_paths.impact: Authenticated access to another tenant's orchestrator context, enabling cross-tenant conversation and document disclosure (TB-5 violation).
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Long-lived tenant API keys are the primary auth mechanism and are frequently leaked in client code and repositories; no MFA is enforced on API-key flows.

attack_paths.entry_point: Tenant authentication endpoint behind the API Gateway (TB-1)
attack_paths.impact: Account takeover of a tenant administrator, granting configuration changes and access to that tenant's conversation history.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Rate Limiter throttles per-IP attempts, but distributed credential stuffing against weak tenant passwords remains feasible.

attack_paths.entry_point: High-volume request flood against LLM completion endpoints (TB-1)
attack_paths.impact: Exhaustion of orchestrator concurrency and third-party model quota, degrading service for all tenants and driving unbounded inference spend.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: LLM completions are expensive and slow; modest request volume can saturate orchestrator worker pools before per-tenant quotas engage.

attack_paths.entry_point: Error responses, debug endpoints, or SSRF from the orchestrator reaching Model Router configuration (TB-4)
attack_paths.impact: Theft of OpenAI and Anthropic API keys, enabling off-platform inference billed to the operator and bypass of all platform guardrails.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Provider keys must be resident in the Model Router process; verbose error handling and shared environment configuration are common leakage vectors.

attack_paths.entry_point: Over-broad orchestrator database role used against the Conversation Store (TB-4)
attack_paths.impact: Bulk exfiltration of confidential conversation history belonging to multiple tenants from a single compromised service identity.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: The orchestrator requires broad read/write on the store; without row-level security a single service-account compromise yields all tenants' data.

attack_paths.entry_point: RAG similarity query issued by the orchestrator without a tenant namespace filter (TB-4, TB-5)
attack_paths.impact: Retrieval of another tenant's embedded documents into the prompt context, which the model then surfaces in its response.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Vector search is the core RAG path and tenant filtering is enforced in application code rather than at the index level, making omission a single-line defect.

attack_paths.entry_point: Prompt-injected instruction causing retrieved context to be encoded into a model request or rendered as a URL in the response (TB-3)
attack_paths.impact: Confidential tenant data is transmitted to an attacker-controlled web service through the trusted model provider egress path.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Model Router egress to provider APIs is allowlisted, but attacker-controlled URLs embedded in model output can be fetched by downstream clients or link previews.

attack_paths.entry_point: Injected instructions establishing a covert channel encoded in prompt/response payloads to a third-party model API (TB-3)
attack_paths.impact: Persistent attacker tasking channel that blends with legitimate model traffic and evades network-layer detection.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Requires sustained injection control and a cooperating external endpoint; Response Filter and egress inspection raise the cost substantially.

attack_paths.entry_point: Tenant document ingestion pipeline writing attacker-controlled embeddings (TB-4)
attack_paths.impact: Manipulated RAG answers for all users of the affected tenant namespace, including falsified policy or pricing guidance.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Ingestion accepts tenant-supplied documents with limited content validation, and embeddings are not integrity-signed.

attack_paths.technique_name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Cloud Logs
attack_paths.entry_point: Compromised orchestrator or Prompt Guard service identity with write access to the Audit Log (TB-4)
attack_paths.impact: Deletion or suppression of request and security events, destroying forensic evidence of prior cross-tenant access.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Audit writes are append-only from a dedicated identity, but the store is not yet WORM-backed and retention policy is enforced in application code.

attack_paths.entry_point: User prompt or retrieved document content passing through Prompt Guard into the orchestrator (TB-2, TB-5)
attack_paths.impact: Goal hijacking of the orchestrator: instruction override, tool/parameter misuse, and cross-tenant context disclosure via the shared model session.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Indirect injection through RAG-ingested documents is not fully separable from legitimate content, and Prompt Guard is a heuristic classifier with known bypasses.

attack_paths.entry_point: Crafted multi-turn prompt sequence submitted through the API Gateway (TB-1, TB-2)
attack_paths.impact: Bypass of system-prompt policy and Response Filter, producing disallowed content or leaking guardrail configuration to the tenant.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Jailbreak techniques evolve faster than static filter rules, and Response Filter operates on a fixed policy set.

attack_paths.entry_point: Prompt instructing the model to reproduce prior context, system prompt, or other tenants' retrieved passages (TB-5)
attack_paths.impact: Disclosure of confidential conversation content and proprietary orchestration instructions to a tenant.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Context windows are shared per request and tenant scoping depends on correct retrieval filtering; leakage is reproducible but requires knowledge of the retrieval layout.

attack_paths.entry_point: Adversarial documents crafted to rank highly for unrelated queries during ingestion (TB-4)
attack_paths.impact: Attacker content is preferentially retrieved and injected into prompts, steering model answers for targeted queries.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Embedding-space manipulation is well documented and requires only document upload rights, which every tenant holds.

attack_paths.entry_point: Compromised fine-tuning dataset or unsigned model artifact loaded by the self-hosted inference host (TB-6)
attack_paths.impact: Persistent trigger-activated behavior in the self-hosted model, silently degrading or biasing responses for all tenants routed to it.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Requires access to the training pipeline or artifact store; artifact signing and provenance checks are planned but not yet enforced.

attack_paths.entry_point: Automated high-token-count requests from many low-privilege or trial tenant accounts (TB-1)
attack_paths.impact: Direct financial loss from third-party inference billing and quota exhaustion that denies service to paying tenants.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: Per-tenant quotas exist but are keyed to accounts, so account multiplication and long-context prompts bypass effective spend ceilings.

attack_paths.entry_point: Iterative extraction prompts sent through Prompt Guard to the orchestrator (TB-2)
attack_paths.impact: Disclosure of proprietary orchestration instructions, guardrail logic, and internal routing hints that enable further bypass.
attack_paths.likelihood_rationale: System prompts are injected into every request and extraction is a well-known technique; Response Filter only partially detects verbatim reproduction.

mitigations.control_name: Strong authentication and authorization on all ingress endpoints
Secure gateway configuration, WAF rules and strict input schema validation
MFA and short-lived tokens for tenant administrator accounts
Per-tenant rate limiting, token budgets and concurrency caps
Encryption at rest with per-tenant KMS keys for all data stores
TLS 1.3 in transit and mTLS between orchestrator and model backends
Secrets vault with scoped, rotatable model provider API keys
Prompt injection defenses: instruction hierarchy, Prompt Guard screening, output policy enforcement
Enforced tenant isolation: row-level security, per-tenant vector namespaces, tenant-scoped service identities
Immutable WORM audit logging with SIEM alerting on cross-tenant access patterns
Vector store integrity: signed embeddings, ingestion content review, retrieval anomaly detection
Model provenance and supply-chain verification with signed model artifacts
Output DLP filtering and egress allowlisting for model provider calls
Per-tenant cost anomaly detection with hard budget caps and account velocity limits
Session and behavioral anomaly detection for tenant accounts
System prompt hardening with secret-free prompts and extraction detection
Network egress proxy with destination allowlist for all model backend traffic

findings.severity_rationale: Indirect prompt injection through RAG content can hijack the shared orchestrator and disclose another tenant's confidential context, breaking the primary multi-tenant isolation guarantee.
Stolen tenant credentials are accepted by the Tenant Router without step-up verification, allowing authenticated cross-tenant access to orchestrator context.
Model provider API keys are resident in the Model Router and reachable through verbose errors or SSRF, giving an attacker off-platform inference and guardrail bypass.
LLM completion endpoints are expensive and slow, so a modest flood saturates orchestrator workers and third-party quota before per-tenant throttles engage.
Tenant-supplied documents are embedded without integrity signing, so manipulated content persistently alters RAG answers for the affected tenant namespace.
A compromised orchestrator identity can suppress audit events, but the dedicated append-only writer identity and SIEM replication limit the scope of evidence loss.
Prompt-injected content can route confidential retrieved context to an attacker-controlled web service through the trusted model egress path, evading network controls.
An unsigned fine-tuned model artifact could carry a persistent trigger backdoor affecting every tenant routed to the self-hosted backend, though pipeline access is restricted.
System prompt extraction discloses orchestration logic and guardrail hints, which is valuable for follow-on bypass but does not directly expose tenant data.
Distributed credential stuffing against tenant logins is partially throttled by the Rate Limiter, limiting but not preventing account takeover.
The orchestrator holds a broad database role over the Conversation Store, so one service-identity compromise yields bulk cross-tenant conversation history.
A covert channel encoded in model API payloads is plausible but requires sustained injection control and a cooperating external endpoint, and egress allowlisting raises cost.
The API Gateway is the only internet-facing component; a memory-safety or request-parsing flaw there bypasses Rate Limiter and Tenant Router entirely.
Tenant scoping for vector retrieval is enforced in application code rather than at the index, so a single missing filter returns another tenant's documents into the prompt.
Jailbreak sequences bypass policy and Response Filter, producing disallowed output and guardrail disclosure without direct cross-tenant data access.
Context-window leakage lets a tenant reproduce other tenants' retrieved passages or prior conversation content, a direct confidentiality breach of the shared orchestrator.
Adversarial documents can be crafted to rank highly for targeted queries, but the effect is scoped to the attacker's own tenant namespace and requires upload rights.
Account multiplication and long-context prompts bypass per-account spend ceilings, causing measurable financial loss and quota starvation for paying tenants.

data_sovereignty: United States (us-east-1, us-west-2) — primary processing and storage
European Union (eu-central-1) — EU tenant conversation and vector data residency
Third-party model inference occurs in the provider's published processing regions (OpenAI US, Anthropic US) under contractual data processing terms

third_party_dependencies.name: Self-Hosted LLM inference service (fine-tuned model artifacts)
Cloud KMS and object storage for data stores and audit retention

tool_call_scope: Vector Database similarity search (read) and document ingestion (write)
Conversation Store read/write for the active tenant
Tenant Config DB read for routing and provider selection
agentic.blast_radius: An uncontrolled orchestrator run can disclose confidential conversation and document content across all tenants sharing the orchestrator, persist poisoned embeddings into the Vector Database that affect all future answers for a tenant, and incur unbounded third-party inference spend. It cannot write to external customer systems, modify model provider infrastructure, or alter KMS key policy; the self-hosted model artifact store is reachable only through the deployment pipeline.
human_oversight_points: Tenant administrator approval required for API key rotation and model routing changes
Prompt Guard and Response Filter rule changes require security review before deployment
No human review of individual agent responses — per-request execution is unsupervised
SOC analyst triage of SIEM alerts for cross-tenant access and audit log anomalies
Model artifact promotion to the self-hosted backend requires release-manager sign-off

model_provenance.provider: Multi-vendor: OpenAI, Anthropic, and self-hosted open-weights model
